doc.title: Tom Scott interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2022 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Session fees, double scale and soloist percentages
summary: He was paid a set fee; they discuss double and triple scale and Phil Woods's Billy Joel story.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Did you get paid a predetermined fee for that particular session?
Phil Woods told a story about how when he did “Just the Way You Are.”
Yeah. He could have got a percentage of every record or something, every 45, as a soloist.
He could have and he didn’t know.
Under what agreement is that? I’ve never of that.
Well I’m going to have to consult Phil if I can.
Oh well that’s going to be tough.
Yes it is. So but isn’t there a thing in I don’t know if it’s the musician’s union but as a soloist don’t you get something beyond what let’s say the bass player gets?

Well in those days many of the A players were getting double scale, in other words, twice as much as was required by the contract between the musician’s union and the recording companies. It was fairly common for the A players to get double scale. And there was a point at which I sometimes asked for and got triple scale. I don’t think in ’73 I had enough credits to demand that. I probably — well if you’re the sole musician on a session you are automatically entitled to double scale because you are designated the leader. The
leader gets double scale. So you know I had yet to rack up a lot of recording credits. And I was just happy to be there, I knew I’d be paid fairly. I probably made double scale for that.
